name: East Ridge (Non-Technical)
approach: From Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road (FR 7601 via Eightmile Road) to the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft). Hike the Stuart Lake Trail roughly 2.5 miles (1,100 ft gain) to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, then switchback up another 1.6 miles (1,100 ft gain) to Colchuck Lake (~4.1 mi, ~2,200 ft total). Continue along the lake's north shore across a boulder field to the base of the Colchuck Glacier.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier to the col, then the ridge west to the summit
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at 3,400 ft, follow the Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction, fork right and switchback up to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft — roughly four miles and 2,200 ft.

Follow the boot path round the lake and across the boulder field at its south end into the basin, then climb the Colchuck Glacier toward the col between Colchuck Peak and Dragontail. Keep climber's right on the glacier to reduce exposure to rockfall coming off Dragontail's north face.

From the col the route is the ridge running west to Colchuck's summit — Class 2-3, hands needed in places, no protection, generally solid granite with good friction.

Navigate from the glacier and the col rather than from a compass bearing off the lake: the peak lies south-west of Colchuck Lake and the col lies south-east of the summit.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep as a scramble; earlier the glacier is a snow climb and wants an axe and crampons
hazards: Rockfall onto the Colchuck Glacier from Dragontail's north face — stay climber's right
Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the glacier
Exposure on the ridge crest despite the easy grade
Wandering off the crest onto steeper flanking ground in poor visibility
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed ridge with no shelter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is the base, and you know you are on it because the ground falls away behind you. Walking up the Colchuck Glacier you are in a closed basin; at the col the far side opens and drops south into the Ingalls Creek drainage. That change from enclosed to open is the arrival, and it happens whether or not you can see anything.

Then turn right. From the col, Colchuck Peak is west and Dragontail is east. The two peaks share this col, so a party that gains it in cloud and turns the wrong way is climbing a different mountain on a different route — and Dragontail's side of the col is not Class 2-3.

The hands test: this ridge is Class 2-3. You will use your hands in places, and you should never need protection or a rope. If you find yourself on ground where you want gear, you have left the crest onto the north or south flank, and the correct answer is to come back to the crest rather than to press on.

Confirmation underfoot: the granite here is solid with good friction, unlike the loose scree of the glacier basin below. Rambling on loose rubble means you are still below the ridge proper.

A warning worth carrying: this is also the standard descent for the harder routes on the peak's north side, so parties will be coming down it. Meeting people descending is not evidence you are on the wrong line — it is evidence you are on the right one.

pitch_detail.notes: ~4.1 mi, ~2,200 ft gain via the Stuart Lake Trail junction and Colchuck Lake Trail switchbacks
Gain the lateral moraine crest above the lake's north shore to avoid loose scree
~550 m gain up the glacier's east (left) lobe; crampons and axe; stay climber's right to avoid Dragontail rockfall
~100 ft of 40° snow, then sandy 3rd-class steps to the 8,500 ft summit plateau and on to the true summit
